etymology:
A deverbal adjective in the קָטִיל (“qatīl”) pattern, from the root מ־ה־ר, the same root as the verb מָהַר (mahár, “to hasten, to hurry, to be quick”). The pattern typically yields adjectives denoting a characteristic disposition, hence “characterized by swiftness.”
Cognate with Arabic مَاهِر (māhir, “skilled, expert”) and its verb مَهَرَ (mahara, “to be skilled, to be proficient”); compare also reflexes of the root in Akkadian, Classical Syriac and Ge'ez denoting skill or training, and Egyptian mhr (“trained warrior”) (per Brown–Driver–Briggs). The inherited sense of swiftness in action developed into that of practised skill, both senses being attested already in Biblical Hebrew.

Alternatively, it is also possible to interpret this noun as originating from the verb יָאַב (ya'áv, “to yearn, desire”) in the pattern מַקְטָל. Those etymological attempts, however, should not be seen as fully credible or conclusive, given that proper nouns of locations and regions tend to be very old reborrowings from multiple languages, and therefore not understandable to speakers of a later language, who try to explain them by folk etymologies or see native compounds in them which don't actually occur.

etymology:
Either of native Semitic origin or borrowed from an Egyptian source. Following the former it is derived from the root כָּנַס (kanás, “to cover, hide”), as the purpose of the priestly undergarments was to further hide the intimate parts (see Exodus 28:42 below). Pants or breeches were more suitable for this, given that tunics and simple cloths were the main ways of dressing oneself in the ancient Mediterranean.
Alternatively, it may go back to an Egyptian derivation as m- + kns (“pubic region”), or merely a borrowing of Egyptian kns whose root was consequently put into the mishkal מִקְטָל to derive the present word.
When pants become more widespread and weren't exclusive to priests the meaning of this word was extended to include all garments having two openings for the legs.

Biblical hapax legomenon derived from שָׁאַב (sha'áv, “to draw water”) and not attested in Mishnaic Hebrew. The original meaning of this word is not conclusive, however two interpretations are possible depending on whether it is to be understood in a passive or active sense. In the former, which is favored by some modern scholars such as Gesenius or Klein and the Vulgata, it refers to watering troughs for cattle, as water was drawn into them (passive sense). The other case interprets the word to refer to something which draws water like a well (active sense) or where water is drawn by someone, and seems to have been the understanding of later Rabbinic commentators. Given that it only occurs inside a poetic and archaic section of the Tanach, it may be reasonable to assume it to have been a more imaginative term for wells and springs or perhaps a neologism to characterize them based on their purpose.
Curiously, all of the extant Greek translation of this passage understand this word to be a pi'el participle in the form of מְשָׁאְבִים (m'sha'evím, “drawers of water”), which could suggest that the Tiberian vocalization might be erroneous.
There's furthermore a lack of unity among the translators as to how to translate this participle, with some manuscripts of the Septuagint rendering it in the most obvious and direct way as ὑδρευόμενοι (hudreuómenoi, “lit. drawers of water”), but other ones deviate by preferring εὐφραινόμενοι (euphrainómenoi, literally “rejoicing”) and Symmachos following suit with συμπίνοντες (sumpínontes, literally “holding a banquet, celebrating”). Aquilas again takes another approach and sees it as καταλέγοντες (katalégontes, literally “telling, narrating”).
The modern meaning as "resource" has its origin in the latter view; just as a well is used for the purpose of drawing water, so are resources used to achieve a certain objective or goal.

Commonly explained as a feminine of עַז (áz, “strong”), but as can be seen from Ancient Greek Γάζα (Gáza) and Arabic غَزَّة (ḡazza), its initial sound was originally Biblical Hebrew *ḡ, from Proto-Semitic *ḡ, so the origin was likely another root. Alternatively compare ج ز ر (j z r) (Hebrew cognate: ג־שׁ־ר), meaning amongst other things words related to “bridge”, a reference to Gaza’s strategic position as the main crossing point on the trade route to Egypt.

From Proto-Semitic *ṣ́abb-. It is likely the word originally referred to some kind of lizard (compare Classical Syriac ܥܒܐ (ʿabbā) and Arabic ضَبّ (ḍabb), both meaning “mastigure”), but its usage in reference to some type of carriage in the Bible led European Jews (who were unfamiliar with the mastigure) to conclude both words must've shared a root relating to "being covered" or "carrying one's possessions around", and thus a connection to tortoises was made.
It is possible that both terms are either unrelated homonyms or are instead related to the Arabic root ض ب ب (ḍ b b) denoting "cleaving to the ground". Nevertheless, the “tortoise” interpretation stuck, with צָב being the ubiquitous term for turtles and tortoises in modern Israeli Hebrew, and neologisms like שַׁלְחוּפָה (ŝalḥūp̄ā) failing to acquire widespread usage.

to mock, to scorn, to scoff
etymology:
The root ק־ל־ס has 3 meanings, "to mock/scorn", "to stomp", and "to laud". The root appears in other Semitic languages as Ugaritic 𐎖𐎍𐎕 (qlṣ /⁠qlṣ⁠/, “to scoff, to mock”), Aramaic קַלֵּס (“to praise, to laud”), Ge'ez ተሳለቀ (täsaläḳä, “to scoff at”), and Arabic قَلَّسَ (qallasa, “to mock, to laud”). Further derivation is unclear, theories include:
* All three senses are derived from Hittite [Term?] (/⁠kalleš-⁠/, “to call, to lure, to invite”), disseminating among Semitic languages as a cultic term whose meaning was later antonymically bifurcated as "to laud" and "to curse/mock/scoff". The sense of "to stomp" might be a derivation of either of the other two senses or the original sense.
* Specifically in regard to the meaning of "to laud", derived from Ancient Greek καλός (kalós, “beautiful, good”); this theory is supported by the geographical and chronological spread of the "to laud" sense.

etymology:
The word רַעַל appears once in the Bible in Zechariah 12:2 and understood there differently by different commentators and translators. Some understand it as "reeling" or "staggering", which corresponds to the Aramaic meaning of the identically-written word, so סף־רעל means "a cup that causes staggering", because it is intoxicating like wine. Others, like Rashi and David Altschuler (Metsudat David), interpreted it as "a killing drug", i.e. poison. The latter became the word's primary meaning in Modern Hebrew.
The modern military slang sense of "morale" is influenced by the expression רוח הלחימה, "fighting spirit", which is abbreviated רה״ל, which, in turn, is pronounced similarly to רעל (see References). The root is perceived to be the same as the root of "poison", so for example, in this context, to "poison" someone (הרעיל) means to boost their morale.

From שבת (“Sabbath, Shabbat, Saturday”). The Hebrew name of the planet is derived from the name of the day of the week, ultimately through analogy with the Roman name for Saturday, which is still named after the Roman god Saturn in some European languages. Originally in Latin the sixth day of the week (seventh in Jewish tradition) was dedicated to the god Saturn (see dies Saturni), but after the Christianization of the Roman Empire it was renamed "Sabbath" (dies Sabbati), as in Hebrew. Today, European languages are split in their name for the day, with the majority using a derivative of שבת, and a few, including English, retaining the dedication to Saturn. The name "שבתאי" is a calque of sorts of the name "Saturn," reinterpreting the planet's name as being taken from the word for Saturday instead of the Roman god.

etymology:
The possessed forms of של were a common Canaanite construction seen also, for example, in Punic 𐤔𐤋𐤉 (šly /⁠sillī⁠/, “my”) and Phoenician 𐤀𐤔 𐤋𐤉 (ʾš ly /⁠ʔas lī⁠/, “my”). These were derived from the relative pronoun *ʔas or prefix *-ʔas in combination with the dative prefix *-l, hence the Hebrew is equivalent to ש־ (she, “which”) + ל־ (l, “to”), thus “which [belongs] to”.
The first use of של as a possessive marker in Hebrew is attested in late parts of the Hebrew Bible, but then still preceded by, and in addition to, a possessive suffix (cf. Canticles 1:6; 3:7). In Mishnaic Hebrew, של־ (shel'-) becomes a true preposition by back-formation. The standalone spelling is a more recent innovation, but the pronoun-including forms are unchanged (which may be seen both in their gemination of the ל, and in the unusual forms of the second- and third-person masculine and feminine plural pronominal suffixes, otherwise found only in the inflections of ל־ (l'-) and ב־ (b'-)).

Ernest Klein connects the term to Hebrew מוד, which is associated with מדד (“to measure”) and the Arabic مَدَّ (madda, “to stretch, prolong”). He also notes that Hommel links it to Arabic تَأْمِيد (taʔmīd, “fixing, establishing”), the verbal noun of أَمَّدَ (ʔammada). Furthermore, Klein reports that Geiger and Peres consider it a contraction of תעמיד, derived from עמד (“to stand”). Conversely, Even-Shoshan identifies מוד as the root and Arabic مَادَ (māda) as a cognate, while also mentioning that some scholars suggest it may be a contraction of תמאיד.

With Nöldeke the Semitic *rayam- is paired with a *rawam- since we have يَرُومُ (yarūmu, “to strive, to aim at”) together with يَرِيمُ (yarīmu, “to depart from”) and Aramaic and Ugaritic show prefix conjugation with both middle -ū- and -ī- in their verb “to get up”, Hebrew only -ū-. etymology: A possible loan relation with Indo-European *ḱr̥h₂-nó-s (“horn”) (from *ḱerh₂- (“horn, head”)) has been suggested, but the direction of loaning is disputed. The term is not to be separated from the root’s ض ر ر (ḍ r r) meaning of “necessity”, the thought being that it was obligatory to take a woman as a wife under particular circumstances, namely when a married brother died without leaving issue, soon also after the root that the family suffered “damage”, which predicament of ill fate is the actual reason why the term bears a faint negative connotation to this day in Arabic, senses of “hostility” or “enmity” leading to the idea of a rival wife not having developed unlike in Ethiopian Semitic and Old South Arabian where they prevail.

etymology:
Said conventionally to be from Ancient Greek σειρᾱ́ (seirā́, “cord, rope; chain”), surely partially for some semantic influence and plurals borrowed from dative plural σειραῖς (seiraîs) and accusative plural σειρᾱ́ς (seirā́s) true, although original Aramaic and Iranian origin is also constructible, see Arabic سَيْر (sayr, “strap”).
CAL groups the sense “construction dust” with better-known Judaeo-Aramaic סׅירָא (sīrā, “thorn”). We don’t know if and how this adds up. “Fine dust” may also come from the idea of a “fine web” or “mesh”. In Robert Payne Smith this is pulvis tenuis next to aranea tenuis, تُرَاب (turāb) and خَيْط الْعَنْكَبُوت (ḵayṭ al-ʕankabūt).
The sense of a “siren” is back-formed from ܣܼܝܪܹܼܝܢ (sīrīn) from Ancient Greek Σειρήν (Seirḗn) understood as absolute state plural, then formally combined with the “rope” word as both being things that draw someone in.
The ichthyonym is kind of obscure, occurring instead emphatic in Jewish Palestinian Aramaic and Jewish Babylonian Aramaic as צִיר (ṣīr, “the own juice wherein fish is conserved; fish brine”) and from this in Arabic صِير (ṣīr). Even the sense of a “strap” has both emphaticities in Arabic, سَيْر (sayr) and صَيْر (ṣayr), supposedly from Aramaic, so one may imagine that the term originally referred to a whole “line” or lure of fish gathered and conceptualized collectively due to the small size of its phenotype.
As we reach the “end” of a fishing line, note also Old Armenian ծայր (cayr, “end; edge”), Old Armenian սայր (sayr, “edge”) and Old Georgian წუერი (c̣ueri, “top; point”).

The underlying root is cognate with Arabic قَنَى (qanā, “to acquire, possess”), Hebrew קָנָה (qānā, “to acquire, buy”), and Ge'ez ቀነየ (qanaya, “to acquire, buy, rule”).

The C-stem causative of 𐩦𐩲𐩧 (s²ʿr, “to be aware; know; perceive”), with the semantic relationship “know, perceive” → “cause to know, make aware”.
Cognate in formation and meaning with Arabic أَشْعَرَ (ʔašʕara, “to make known, inform, notify”); compare Yemeni Arabic أَشْعَرَ (ʔašʕara, “to let know”). The underlying perception root is also represented by Minaean 𐩦𐩲𐩧 (s²ʿr, “to be aware”) and the related Ḥaḍramitic 𐩦𐩩𐩲𐩧 (s²tʿr, “to recognize, become aware”).

glosses: Infinitive form of 𐩠𐩦𐩲𐩧 (hs²ʿr, “to inform; make known; communicate”).
etymology:
An infinitival form of 𐩠𐩦𐩲𐩧 (hs²ʿr, “to inform; make known”), the C-stem causative of 𐩦𐩲𐩧 (s²ʿr, “to know; be aware”).
The causative corresponds closely to Arabic أَشْعَرَ (ʔašʕara, “to make known, inform, notify”) and Yemeni Arabic أَشْعَرَ (ʔašʕara, “to let know”). Compare also Minaean 𐩦𐩲𐩧 (s²ʿr, “to be aware”) for the underlying G-stem.

glosses: To cause something to be built or constructed; to have or order a structure built.
etymology:
The C-stem of 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “to build, construct”), expressing causation or commissioned construction.
Compare Qatabanian 𐩪𐩨𐩧𐩱 (s¹brʾ, “to cause to be built, have constructed”). The contrast between the Sabaean-type h- causative and the Qatabanian s¹- causative is morphologically significant.
At the root level compare Arabic بَرَأَ (baraʔa, “to create”), بَرَى (barā, “to fashion or shape by cutting”), and Hebrew בָּרָא (bārāʾ, “to create”).

glosses: To settle or discharge a debt.
To release someone from a financial obligation or claim.
etymology:
The C-stem of the legal 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “to be free from liability; settle an obligation”) family.
Compare Arabic أَبْرَأَ (ʔabraʔa, “to release from a claim or debt, acquit”), Harsusi abrō (“to free from debt or guilt”), Jibbali ebréʾ (“to declare innocent, free from obligation”), and Mehri abōri (“to free from guilt or debt”). Yemeni Arabic ʾabrā likewise means “forego, renounce, remit”.

glosses: to appropriate; to take possession of; to make oneself master of something.
to seize; to capture or take enemy property, towns, territories, or strongholds.
to conquer; to subdue; to bring under direct control.
to gain control of a city, land, people, or military objective.
etymology:
C-stem of 𐩨𐩲𐩡 (bʿl, “to possess; own; be lord of”), from Proto-Semitic *baʿl- (“owner; lord; master”). Compare Akkadian 𒂗 (bēlu, “lord, owner”), Ugaritic 𐎁𐎓𐎍 (bʿl, “lord; Baal”), Hebrew בַּעַל (baʿal, “owner, lord”), Arabic بَعْل (baʕl, “lord, husband”), Ge'ez በዓል (baʿāl, “owner, master”), Harsusi bāl (“master, lord; possessor”), Mehri bāl (“owner, possessor”), and Shehri báʿal (“person owning or in charge of something”).

Note: 𐩠𐩨𐩲𐩡 (hbʿl) belongs to the ownership and control branch of the root. In royal and military inscriptions it often means “to seize”, “to take possession of”, or “to bring under control”.

glosses: infinitive of 𐩠𐩨𐩲𐩡 (hbʿl, “to appropriate; seize; take possession of; bring under control”).
etymology: From 𐩠𐩨𐩲𐩡 (hbʿl, “to appropriate; seize; take possession of”), the C-stem of 𐩨𐩲𐩡 (bʿl, “to possess; own; be lord of”), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *baʿl- (“owner; lord; master”).

glosses: Remote demonstrative pronoun: that, that one.
Third-person singular independent pronoun: he, she, it.
etymology:
From the Sabaean remote-deictic pronoun system. Related to 𐩠𐩥𐩩 (hwt), 𐩠𐩺𐩩 (hyt), 𐩠𐩣𐩥 (hmw), and 𐩠𐩬 (hn).
Compare the wider Semitic third-person pronominal base reflected in Arabic هُوَ (huwa, “he”), Arabic هِيَ (hiya, “she”), Hebrew הוּא (hū, “he”), and Hebrew הִיא (hī, “she”).

glosses: fortified settlement; walled or defended urban settlement.
settlement; inhabited site or built-up place, often of variable size.
settled territory; urban district or domain attached to a city.
city-dwellers; townspeople; sedentary population, as opposed to nomads or Arabs.
etymology:
Probably inherited within South Semitic settlement vocabulary. Compare Ge'ez ሀገር (hagar, “city, town, village, province, district, country, homeland”). Also compare Qatabanian 𐩠𐩴𐩧 (hgr, “city, town”), Minaic 𐩠𐩴𐩧 (hgr, “city, town”), and Hadramitic 𐩠𐩴𐩧 (hgr, “city, town”).

Note: Sabaweb gives the main noun as “city”. The older translation record includes city, town, fortified settlement, oppidum, citadel, settled territory, and urban settlement. A separate but related Sabaweb record gives “city-dwellers, townspeople, sedentary people”.

glosses: Feminine singular oblique form of the remote demonstrative: that, that one, the aforementioned.
Oblique third-person singular feminine independent-pronoun form: her, it, that one.
etymology: From the Sabaean remote-deictic pronoun system. Sabaweb lists 𐩠𐩺𐩩 (hyt) under 𐩠𐩺𐩱𐩰 (hyʾf) as a feminine singular oblique form of the remote demonstrative.

glosses: Before a prefix-conjugation verb, marking jussive, directive, or optative force: may, let, must, should.
With a following clause-introducing particle, especially 𐩹𐩩 (ḏt), introducing reason or purpose: because, so that, for that.
etymology:
Cognate with Arabic لِـ (li-, “to, for”), Hebrew לְ־ (lə-, “to, for”), Aramaic ל־ (l-, “to, for”), and Ge'ez ለ (la-, “to, for”).
The jussive and optative use belongs to a wider Semitic pattern of *l- (“modal or directive particle”) before finite verbal forms; compare 𒇻 (lū, “may, let”).

glosses: to, towards; marking direction, goal, or movement toward a point.
for, for the benefit of; marking recipient, beneficiary, purpose, or dative relation.
belonging to, of; marking possession or association.
on, at; introducing dates or time expressions, especially in dating formulae.
Before an infinitive or verbal noun, marking purpose: in order to, so as to.
etymology:
Cognate with Arabic لِـ (li-, “to, for”), Hebrew לְ־ (lə-, “to, for”), Aramaic ל־ (l-, “to, for”), and Ge'ez ለ (la-, “to, for”).
The jussive and optative use belongs to a wider Semitic pattern of *l- (“modal or directive particle”) before finite verbal forms; compare 𒇻 (lū, “may, let”).
From Proto-Semitic *lišān-.

glosses: since, after, when; introducing a temporal clause with a following verb.
since, after, from the time that; introducing a temporal clause with a following clause-introducing particle.
etymology: Probably a lexicalized combination of 𐩡 (l-) and the enclitic or connective element 𐩬 (-n). Sabaweb compares the formation of 𐩨𐩬 (bn) from 𐩨 (b-) plus 𐩬 (-n). Compare inscriptional Ethiopic ln (“from”).

glosses: from, away from; marking a starting point, source, or point of departure.
from, since; marking a spatial or temporal starting-point, often with a following endpoint introduced by 𐩲𐩵 (ʿd) or 𐩲𐩵𐩺 (ʿdy).
along, from along; in spatial extent expressions.
along; formerly taken as a separate prepositional value in some readings, but usually better understood as the ordinary preposition “from”.
etymology: Probably a lexicalized combination of 𐩡 (l-) and the enclitic or connective element 𐩬 (-n). Sabaweb compares the formation of 𐩨𐩬 (bn) from 𐩨 (b-) plus 𐩬 (-n). Compare inscriptional Ethiopic ln (“from”).

glosses: harm, damage, evil; an undesirable event or misfortune.
etymology: Uncertain. Sabaweb treats this as a separate lexical item from the preposition and conjunction above.
From Proto-Semitic *ḥimār- (“donkey”).
Inherited from Proto-West Semitic *ḥyḳ- (“shore”).

glosses: king, ruler, part of a royal tributary
owner, proprietor, one who owns or has a property
etymology: From Proto-Semitic *malk- (“king, prince”).
From Proto-Semitic *malk- (“king, prince”).

glosses: to become or be king, to rule, to govern
etymology: From Proto-Semitic *malk- (“king, prince”).

glosses: to make (s.o.) king, to appoint (s.o.) as king
sacred precinct; consecrated or protected sacred enclosure.
cultic complex; sacred area of a deity, including the temple and associated precinct or protected space.
divine sanctuary or temple of a named deity.
temple or sacred precinct in which ritual restrictions apply.
etymology:
A place noun built on the inherited Semitic root *ḥ-r-m (“to forbid; make sacred; set apart”). Compare Arabic حَرَم (ḥaram, “sacred precinct, sanctuary”), Arabic حَرَام (ḥarām, “forbidden; sacred”), Hebrew חֵרֶם (ḥērem, “ban; devoted thing”), Ge'ez ሐረመ (ḥarama, “to forbid; consecrate”), Ge'ez ምሕራም (məḥrām, “sanctuary, shrine”), Mehri ḥərōm (“taboo, forbidden”), Harsusi ḥerōm (“forbidden, taboo”), and Shehri ḥárúm (“forbidden”). Also compare Qatabanian 𐩣𐩢𐩧𐩣 (mḥrm, “sanctuary”), Minaic 𐩣𐩢𐩧𐩣 (mḥrm, “sacred area; sanctuary”), and Hadramitic 𐩣𐩢𐩧𐩣 (mḥrm, “sanctuary”).

 Compare Arabic حَرَم (ḥaram, “sacred precinct”), Hebrew חֵרֶם (ḥērem, “ban”), Ge'ez ምሕራም (məḥrām, “sanctuary”), Mehri ḥərōm (“taboo, forbidden”), Harsusi ḥerōm (“forbidden, taboo”), Shehri ḥárúm (“forbidden”)
Note: Sabaweb gives 𐩣𐩢𐩧𐩣 (mḥrm) as “sanctuary; temple”. The term may denote a temple building, a sacred precinct, or a wider protected cultic complex, depending on context.

glosses: An agricultural or hydraulic installation, perhaps a cistern.
etymology:
A nominal formation belonging to the QNY property vocabulary, ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”), with prefix m- and final -t.
Compare Hebrew מִקְנֶה (miqne, “property, livestock”). The precise morphological relationship of the Sabaean formation is uncertain.

glosses: property, possession; something owned or held.
etymology:
An m- nominal formation from the QNY acquisition and possession vocabulary, ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”).
Compare Hebrew מִקְנֶה (miqne, “property, livestock”) and Arabic قَنَى (qanā, “to acquire, possess”).
From Proto-Semitic *may-.

glosses: A boat, ship, or other waterborne vessel.
A fleet or group of vessels.
etymology:
An m- nominal formation from the Semitic root 𐩧𐩫𐩨 (rkb, “to ride”), extending the idea of “that which is ridden or boarded” to a means of transport.
Cognate with Arabic مَرْكَب (markab, “vehicle; boat, ship”), Ge'ez መርከብ (märkäb, “boat, ship”), and related to Classical Syriac ܡܰܪܟܰܒܬܳܐ (markabtā, “vehicle, chariot”) and Hebrew מֶרְכָּבָה (merkavá, “chariot, carriage”).
Modern South Arabian preserves especially close forms: Harsusi márkeb (“ship”), Shehri mɛrkɛb (“boat”), and Mehri mərkēb (“boat”). Compare also Yemeni Arabic مَرْكَب (markab, “ship, steamer”).

glosses: A caravan, travelling convoy, or similar organized travelling group.
etymology:
An m-...-t nominal formation of the Semitic root 𐩧𐩫𐩨 (rkb, “to ride”), belonging to the same transport vocabulary as 𐩣𐩧𐩫𐩨 (mrkb, “boat, ship”).
Compare Arabic رَكِبَ (rakiba, “to ride, mount, board”), the closely formed Arabic مَرْكَبَة (markaba, “vehicle, carriage”), and Geʿez ረከበ (räkäbä, “to ride; go by boat”). Further compare Harsusi rēkeb (“to mount, ride”), Shehri rékəb (“to ride, mount”), and Mehri rēkēb (“to ride, mount”).
The exact relationship between the formation and a particular type of travelling group is not fully recoverable.

glosses: singular construct-state form of 𐩣𐩨𐩧𐩱𐩣 (mbrʾm, “construction, building work”)
singular form of 𐩣𐩨𐩧𐩱𐩣 (mbrʾm, “construction, building work”) in the pronominal-suffix state
etymology: A construct- and pronominal-suffix-state form of 𐩣𐩨𐩧𐩱𐩣 (mbrʾm, “construction, building work”).

glosses: A legal act, status or transaction associated with settlement, discharge or freedom from an obligation.
etymology:
An m- formation of the legal BRʾ family. Its precise lexical function remains uncertain.
Compare Arabic مُبَرَّأ (mubarraʔ, “free from liability, cleared”) and بَرِيء (barīʔ, “free of liability, innocent”), Harsusi berīʾ (“free of debt, innocent”), Jibbali bíríʾ (“free, innocent”), and Mehri bəráyʾ (“innocent, free of debt or responsibility”).
Yemeni Arabic likewise preserves barī “exempt, innocent”.

An m- nominal formation of the architectural 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “to build, construct”) family.
Cognate with Qatabanian 𐩣𐩨𐩧𐩱 (mbrʾ, “construction, building or irrigation work”) and Hadrami 𐩣𐩨𐩧𐩱 (mbrʾ, “construction, building work”).
At the root level compare Arabic بَرَأَ (baraʔa, “to create”) and بَرَى (barā, “to fashion or shape by cutting”), together with Hebrew בָּרָא (bārāʾ, “to create, bring forth”).

glosses: singular indeterminate-state form of 𐩣𐩨𐩧𐩱 (mbrʾ, “legal act or state associated with settlement or discharge”)
etymology: Indeterminate-state form of the separate legal noun 𐩣𐩨𐩧𐩱 (mbrʾ), whose precise referent is uncertain but belongs to the BRʾ vocabulary of freedom from liability and settlement of obligations.

A t-final nominal formation of the architectural BRʾ family, lexically distinguished by Sabaweb from the identically written plural form of 𐩣𐩨𐩧𐩱𐩣 (mbrʾm, “construction, building work”) treated below.
Compare Arabic بَرَأَ (baraʔa, “to create”) and بَرَى (barā, “to fashion or shape by cutting”), together with Hebrew בָּרָא (bārāʾ, “to create, bring forth”).

glosses: plural construct-state form of 𐩣𐩨𐩧𐩱𐩣 (mbrʾm, “construction, building work”)
plural form of 𐩣𐩨𐩧𐩱𐩣 (mbrʾm, “construction, building work”) in the pronominal-suffix state
etymology: A plural state form of 𐩣𐩨𐩧𐩱𐩣 (mbrʾm, “construction, building work”).

glosses: singular determinate-state form of 𐩣𐩨𐩧𐩱𐩣 (mbrʾm, “construction, building work”)
etymology: From 𐩣𐩨𐩧𐩱𐩣 (mbrʾm, “construction, building work”) with the determinate-state ending -n.

glosses: property; possession; thing or estate owned.
estate; property-domain, especially land or productive property attached to a deity or temple.
assets; wealth; funds or resources under someone’s control.
temple property; property belonging to a deity, temple, or cultic estate.
etymology:
From the root 𐩨𐩲𐩡 (bʿl, “to own; possess; be lord of”), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *baʿl- (“owner; lord; master”), with nominal prefix 𐩣 (m-). Compare Ge'ez ብዕል (bəʿl, “wealth, riches”), Shehri baʿál (“to own, take ownership of”), and Mehri mābáyl (“owned”).

 Related terms 𐩨𐩲𐩡 (bʿl, “lord; owner”), 𐩨𐩲𐩡𐩩 (bʿlt, “lady; mistress”), 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “property, possession”), 𐩣𐩤𐩬𐩺 (mqny, “property, possession”), 𐩨𐩺𐩩 (byt, “house; estate; temple”)
 Compare Akkadian 𒂗 (bēlu, “lord, owner”), Ugaritic 𐎁𐎓𐎍 (bʿl, “lord; Baal”), Hebrew בַּעַל (baʿal, “owner, lord”), Arabic بَعْل (baʕl, “lord, husband”), Ge'ez ብዕል (bəʿl, “wealth, riches”), Mehri mābáyl (“owned”), Harsusi baʿál (“to own”)
Note: 𐩣𐩨𐩲𐩡 (mbʿl) denotes property or assets under ownership or control. In cultic contexts it often refers to the estate or property of a deity or temple.

glosses: title of an unidentified official or functionary.
honorific expression, possibly “your honour” or “your authority”, especially in the pronominal-suffix form 𐩣𐩨𐩲𐩡𐩫 (mbʿlk).
etymology: Uncertain. Sabaweb lists a separate 𐩣𐩨𐩲𐩡 (mbʿl) as a title of an unidentified functionary, explicitly distinguished from 𐩣𐩨𐩲𐩡 (mbʿl, “property, estate”) above. It is probably related to the same 𐩨𐩲𐩡 (bʿl) ownership and lordship family, but the exact office is not clear.

glosses: singular indeterminate-state form of 𐩣𐩨𐩲𐩡 (mbʿl, “property; estate; assets”)
etymology: From 𐩣𐩨𐩲𐩡 (mbʿl, “property; estate; assets”), from the root 𐩨𐩲𐩡 (bʿl, “to own; possess; be lord of”), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *baʿl- (“owner; lord; master”).

glosses: indeterminate singular form of 𐩣𐩨𐩲𐩡 (mbʿl, “title or honorific expression”).
etymology: From 𐩣𐩨𐩲𐩡 (mbʿl), a rare uncertain title or honorific expression connected with the root 𐩨𐩲𐩡 (bʿl, “lord; owner”). Sabaweb distinguishes this use from 𐩣𐩨𐩲𐩡 (mbʿl, “property; estate; assets”).

glosses: pronominal-suffix form of 𐩣𐩨𐩲𐩡 (mbʿl, “authority; honour; title”), with second masculine singular suffix; your authority; your honour.
etymology:
From 𐩣𐩨𐩲𐩡 (mbʿl), a rare title, honorific expression, or term of authority connected with the root 𐩨𐩲𐩡 (bʿl, “lord; owner”), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *baʿl- (“owner; lord; master”), with the second masculine singular pronominal suffix 𐩫 (-k, “your”).
Sabaweb treats this use of 𐩣𐩨𐩲𐩡 (mbʿl) separately from 𐩣𐩨𐩲𐩡 (mbʿl, “property; estate; assets”).

glosses: singular determinate-state form of 𐩣𐩨𐩲𐩡 (mbʿl, “property; estate; assets”)
etymology:
From 𐩣𐩨𐩲𐩡 (mbʿl, “property; estate; assets”), from the root 𐩨𐩲𐩡 (bʿl, “to own; possess; be lord of”), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *baʿl- (“owner; lord; master”).
The form 𐩣𐩨𐩲𐩡𐩬 (mbʿln) is the determinate singular form of the property noun.

glosses: before, against; marking separation, opposition, or protection from something harmful.
etymology:
Cognate with Arabic مِنْ (min, “from”), Hebrew מִן (min, “from”), Aramaic מִן (min, “from”), and Ge'ez እም (ʾəm, “from”).
In Sabaean, this form is much less central than 𐩨𐩬 (bn), which is the ordinary preposition “from”. Sabaweb describes prepositional 𐩣𐩬 (mn) as an Arabising equivalent of 𐩨𐩬 (bn).

glosses: who, whoever, anyone who; relative or indefinite pronoun.
etymology: Cognate with Arabic مَنْ (man, “who, whoever”), Aramaic מַן (man, “who”), and Akkadian 𒈠𒀭𒉡 (mannu, “who”).
Compare Akkadian maḫārum (“to accept, receive”) and Soqotri meḥor (“to offer”).

glosses: plural indeterminate-state form of 𐩣𐩹𐩠𐩨𐩩 (mḏhbt, “agricultural installation; irrigation structure”)
An agricultural installation or irrigation structure.
A water-management feature associated with an irrigation system.
etymology: From the water and irrigation branch of 𐩹𐩠𐩨 (ḏhb), connected with flood-water, irrigation, and irrigated land.

From Proto-Semitic *ḳarib- (“to be near, be close; to approach”).
Cognate with Minaean 𐩤𐩧𐩨 (qrb, “to approach, come near”), Akkadian 𒆪𒉡 (qerēbu, “to be near, come near”), Ugaritic 𐎖𐎗𐎁 (qrb, “to approach, be close to”), Hebrew קָרַב (qāraḇ, “to approach”), Classical Syriac ܩܪܶܒ (qəreḇ, “to come near”), Arabic قَرِبَ (qariba, “to be near, approach”), Ge'ez ቀረበ (ḳäräbä, “to be near, come near”), Harsusi ḳēreb (“to be near, come near”), Shehri ḳérəb (“to be near”), and Mehri ḳáyrəb (“to approach, be near”). Compare also Safaitic qrb (“soon; near”).

From Proto-Semitic *ḳarib- (“to be near, be close; to approach”).
Cognate with Minaean 𐩤𐩧𐩨 (qrb, “to approach, come near”), Akkadian 𒆪𒉡 (qerēbu, “to be near, come near”), Ugaritic 𐎖𐎗𐎁 (qrb, “to approach, be close to”), Hebrew קָרַב (qāraḇ, “to approach”), Classical Syriac ܩܪܶܒ (qəreḇ, “to come near”), Arabic قَرِبَ (qariba, “to be near, approach”), Ge'ez ቀረበ (ḳäräbä, “to be near, come near”), Harsusi ḳēreb (“to be near, come near”), Shehri ḳérəb (“to be near”), and Mehri ḳáyrəb (“to approach, be near”). Compare also Safaitic qrb (“soon; near”).

glosses: To be near, close; to approach, come near.
etymology:
From Proto-Semitic *ḳarib- (“to be near, be close; to approach”).
Cognate with Minaean 𐩤𐩧𐩨 (qrb, “to approach, come near”), Akkadian 𒆪𒉡 (qerēbu, “to be near, come near”), Ugaritic 𐎖𐎗𐎁 (qrb, “to approach, be close to”), Hebrew קָרַב (qāraḇ, “to approach”), Classical Syriac ܩܪܶܒ (qəreḇ, “to come near”), Arabic قَرِبَ (qariba, “to be near, approach”), Ge'ez ቀረበ (ḳäräbä, “to be near, come near”), Harsusi ḳēreb (“to be near, come near”), Shehri ḳérəb (“to be near”), and Mehri ḳáyrəb (“to approach, be near”). Compare also Safaitic qrb (“soon; near”).

glosses: To bring near, bring to someone.
etymology: The D-stem of 𐩤𐩧𐩨 (qrb, “to be near, approach”), with the transitive development “cause to approach, bring near” → “bring, send, deliver”. Compare Proto-Semitic *ḳarrib- (“to bring, offer”), Arabic قَرَّبَ (qarraba, “to bring near, present, offer”), Yemeni Arabic garrab “bring near, bring something to someone”, and Shehri eḳórub (“to bring near, nearer”).

glosses: Indeterminate singular form of 𐩤𐩧𐩨 (qrb, “near, close”).
etymology: From the adjective 𐩤𐩧𐩨 (qrb, “near, close”) with the indeterminate-state ending -m.

glosses: Third-person masculine plural suffix-conjugation form of 𐩤𐩧𐩨 (qrb, “to be near, approach”).
etymology: From the G-stem 𐩤𐩧𐩨 (qrb, “to be near, approach”) with third-person masculine plural agreement.

glosses: Third-person masculine plural suffix-conjugation form of 𐩤𐩧𐩨 (qrb, “to bring near, bring, send”).
etymology: From the D-stem 𐩤𐩧𐩨 (qrb, “to bring near, bring, send”) with third-person masculine plural agreement.

glosses: Third-person feminine singular suffix-conjugation form of 𐩤𐩧𐩨 (qrb, “to be near, approach”).
etymology: From 𐩤𐩧𐩨 (qrb, “to be near, approach”) with third-person feminine singular agreement.

glosses: Determinate singular form of 𐩤𐩧𐩨 (qrb, “near, close”).
etymology: From the adjective 𐩤𐩧𐩨 (qrb, “near, close”) with the determinate-state ending -n.

glosses: offering, sacrifice; something presented as an offering.
etymology:
A religious nominal formation of the QRB “approach, bring near, present” family.
Compare Hebrew קָרְבָּן (qorbān, “offering, sacrifice”), Classical Syriac ܩܘܪܒܢܐ (qurbānā, “offering, sacrifice”), Geʿez ቍርባን (ḳʷərban, “offering, sacrifice”), and Arabic قُرْبَان (qurbān, “sacrifice, offering”).

glosses: Absolute singular form of 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt, “qnt-measure; capacity measure”).
etymology:
A shorter absolute-state form of the 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt, “qnt-measure”) lexeme. Its contexts consist of measurements of grain comparable to those containing 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt), which supports their identification as forms of the same measure-name.
The parent lexeme is also attested as Qatabanian 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt), Minaean 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt), and Ḥaḍramitic 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt). The historical explanation of the Sabaean alternation qnt ~ qt remains uncertain.

glosses: singular form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩣 (qnym, “possession, property”) in the pronominal-suffix state
etymology: A shortened pronominal-state variant of 𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩣 (qnym, “possession, property”), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”).

glosses: plural indeterminate-state form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “small livestock, sheep”)
etymology: An alternative indeterminate plural formation of 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “small livestock, sheep”), from the inherited QNY possession/livestock vocabulary, ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”).

glosses: A unit or standard of dry capacity; a qnt-measure.
etymology:
The same measure-name is found across Old South Arabian. Compare Qatabanian 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt, “measure vessel, capacity measure”), Minaean 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt, “capacity measure”), and Ḥaḍramitic 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt, “measure of capacity or weight”).
Its deeper origin is uncertain. Comparisons have been made with Amharic ቁና (qunnā, “grain measure; measuring basket”), Tigrē qannana “to measure grain”, and ōḳən (“to measure”). These have prompted a possible connection with a root wqn ~ qn, although the Shehri verb can refer to measuring size or fit rather than specifically measuring capacity.
Arabic ʾuqna, wuqna “a bird's place, nest” and Yemeni Arabic mawqana, referring to large stones or hollows in which grain is threshed, have also been compared on semantic grounds. Their relationship to 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt) is uncertain.
An older proposal compared the measure-name with Greek κεντηνάριον “hundredweight”; this derivation has not been established.

glosses: singular indeterminate-state form of 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt, “qnt-measure; capacity measure”)
etymology:
From 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt, “qnt-measure; capacity measure”) with the indeterminate-state ending -m.
The underlying measure-name has direct Old South Arabian parallels in Qatabanian 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt), Minaean 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt), and Ḥaḍramitic 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt). More distant comparisons include Amharic ቁና (qunnā, “grain measure; measuring basket”), Tigrē qannana “to measure grain”, and ōḳən (“to measure”).

glosses: singular determinate-state form of 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt, “qnt-measure; capacity measure”)
etymology:
From 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt, “qnt-measure; capacity measure”) with the determinate-state ending -n.
The measure-name is shared with Qatabanian 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt), Minaean 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt), and Ḥaḍramitic 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt). Possible wider comparisons include Amharic ቁና (qunnā, “grain measure; measuring basket”), Tigrē qannana “to measure grain”, and ōḳən (“to measure”).

glosses: A royal qnt-measure; a royal standard of the 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt) capacity measure.
etymology:
A construct expression from 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt, “qnt-measure; capacity measure”) + 𐩣𐩡𐩫𐩬 (mlkn, “the king”), literally “the qnt-measure of the king”, hence “royal qnt-measure”.
The measure-name has direct Old South Arabian parallels in Qatabanian 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt), Minaean 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt), and Ḥaḍramitic 𐩤𐩬𐩩 (qnt).
The second element belongs to the widespread Semitic word for “king”; compare Arabic مَلِك (malik, “king”), Hebrew מֶלֶךְ (melekh, “king”), and Classical Syriac ܡܠܟܐ (malkā, “king”).

glosses: To acquire, obtain, take possession of; to possess, own.
To obtain offspring; to beget or bear children.
etymology:
Ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”). Cognate with Qatabanian Qatabanian 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “to acquire, possess”), Minaean Minaean 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “to acquire, possess”), and Ḥaḍramitic Hadrami 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “to acquire, possess”), as well as Arabic قَنَى (qanā, “to acquire, possess”), Hebrew קָנָה (qānā, “to acquire, buy”), and Ge'ez ቀነየ (qanaya, “to acquire, buy, rule”). Compare Akkadian 𒅗𒉡 (qanû, “to acquire, keep”).
The extension from acquisition to obtaining or producing offspring has ancient Semitic parallels. Compare Ugaritic 𐎖𐎐𐎊 (qny, “to create, establish”); the Sabaean childbearing use is independently attested both of acquiring children and of a woman bearing children.

glosses: To cause someone to acquire something; to give into possession, transfer ownership.
etymology:
A homographic verbal formation belonging to the same inherited QNY family, ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”). It has been analysed as a transitive or causative-like development “cause to acquire” → “give into possession, transfer ownership”.
Its delimitation from the ordinary G-stem and from 𐩠𐩤𐩬𐩺 (hqny, “to dedicate, consecrate”) is not always secure. Some passages assigned to this verb have instead been interpreted as ordinary QNY, particularly in the childbearing sense, or as erroneous spellings for the C-stem.

glosses: singular construct-state form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩣 (qnym, “possession, property”)
singular form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩣 (qnym, “possession, property”) in the pronominal-suffix state
etymology: A construct- and pronominal-state form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩣 (qnym, “possession, property”), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”).

glosses: small livestock, especially sheep; in livestock documents, particularly a ewe.
etymology:
A specialised nominal use of the inherited QNY possession vocabulary, ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”), with the semantic development “property, possessions” → “livestock”.
Compare Minaean 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “small livestock, sheep”) and Yemeni Arabic qanāya ~ qanīya “small herd kept at home”.

glosses: possession, property; collectively, possessions, goods, assets.
etymology:
From the inherited QNY acquisition vocabulary, ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”).
Direct Old South Arabian parallels include Qatabanian 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “property, possessions”), Minaean 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “property, possessions”), and Ḥaḍramitic 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “property, possession”). Compare Hebrew קִנְיָן (qinyān, “possession, property”) and the verbal cognates Arabic قَنَى (qanā, “to acquire, possess”) and Hebrew קָנָה (qānā, “to acquire, buy”).

glosses: singular indeterminate-state form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “small livestock, sheep”)
plural indeterminate-state form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “small livestock, sheep”)
etymology: An indeterminate-state form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “small livestock, sheep”), itself a specialised development of the inherited QNY possession vocabulary.

glosses: Third-person masculine plural suffix-conjugation form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “to acquire, possess; obtain offspring”).
etymology: From 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “to acquire, possess; obtain offspring”), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”).

glosses: Third-person masculine plural suffix-conjugation form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “to cause to acquire; give into possession”).
etymology: Also source-listed as a third-person masculine plural form of the homographic QNY verb “cause to acquire; give into possession”.

glosses: Third-person feminine singular suffix-conjugation form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “to acquire, possess; bear or obtain offspring”).
etymology: From 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “to acquire, possess; bear or obtain offspring”), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”).

glosses: Third-person feminine singular suffix-conjugation form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “to cause to acquire; give into possession”).
etymology: The same ATHS 4/4 spelling is also indexed in Sabaweb under the separate QNY verb “cause to acquire; give into possession”. The two analyses should not be treated as simultaneously certain.

glosses: Third-person feminine dual suffix-conjugation form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “to acquire, possess”).
etymology: From 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “to acquire, possess”), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”).

glosses: singular determinate-state form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩣 (qnym, “possession, property”)
etymology: From 𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩣 (qnym, “possession, property”) with the determinate-state ending -n. The parent lexeme is ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”).

glosses: plural determinate-state form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “small livestock, sheep”)
etymology: A determinate plural form of the livestock noun 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “small livestock, sheep”).

glosses: Infinitive of 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “to cause to acquire; give into possession”).
etymology: Infinitive of the homographic verb “cause to acquire; give into possession”, ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”).

glosses: Third-person feminine plural suffix-conjugation form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “to acquire, possess”).
etymology: From 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “to acquire, possess”), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”).

glosses: and; also; as well as; together with.
but, whereas; marking contrast or a turn in the discourse.
then, and then; marking continuation in a narrative or formulaic sequence.
Used to introduce a clause, predicate, apodosis, or new textual unit, often left untranslated in English.
etymology: Cognate with Arabic وَ (wa, “and”), Ge'ez ወ (wa-, “and”), Harami w(e)- (“and”), and Mehri w- (“and”). Compare also Proto-Semitic *wa- (“and”).

glosses: children; descendants; members descended from or belonging to a family, clan, lineage, or social group.
“sons” or dependants of a deity; members of a cultic community, tribal community, or confederation associated with a deity.
etymology:
From Proto-Semitic *w-l-d (“to give birth; bear”). Compare Arabic وَلَد (walad, “child, son”), Ge'ez ወልድ (wald, “son, child”), and Hebrew יֶלֶד (yeled, “child”).

glosses: to give birth; to bear or bring forth a child or young animal.
etymology:
From Proto-Semitic *w-l-d (“to give birth; bear”). Compare Arabic وَلَد (walad, “child, son”), Ge'ez ወልድ (wald, “son, child”), and Hebrew יֶלֶד (yeled, “child”).

glosses: grassland, bushland, wilderness; uncultivated or vegetated country.
etymology:
A nominal formation belonging to a Semitic vegetation and landscape word-family. Compare Arabic شَعْرَى (šaʕrā, “maquis, bush-covered country”), Ge'ez ሣዕር (śāʿr, “herb, grass, vegetation, meadow, pasture”), and Yemeni Arabic شَعْرَى (šaʕrā, “untilled land”).
Arabic also has šaʿār for dense or luxuriant trees. The vegetation and landscape parallels favour the interpretation “grassland, bushland, wilderness” over the older interpretation “sanctuary”; the latter may have been encouraged by comparison with Arabic šaʿīra “religious rite; cult place”.

From 𐩦𐩲𐩧 (s²ʿr, “barley”) with the indeterminate-state ending -m.
The lexical base is cognate with Minaean 𐩦𐩲𐩧 (s²ʿr, “barley”), Arabic شَعِير (šaʕīr, “barley”), Hebrew שְׂעוֹרָה (śəʿōrā, “barley”), and Classical Syriac ܣܥܪܬܐ (səʿārtā, “barley”); compare Yemeni Arabic شَعِير (šaʕīr, “barley”).

Also compare Qatabanian 𐩦𐩺𐩣 (s²ym, “divine patron”), Minaic 𐩦𐩺𐩣 (s²ym, “divine patron”), and Ḥaḍramitic 𐩦𐩺𐩣 (s²ym, “patron”).

glosses: To ride, mount; to ride an animal.
etymology:
From the inherited Semitic root √RKB denoting riding, mounting, and travel by a conveyance. Cognate with Akkadian Akkadian rakābu (“to ride; travel by vehicle”), Arabic رَكِبَ (rakiba, “to ride, mount; embark”), Hebrew רָכַב (rāḵaḇ, “to ride”), Ugaritic 𐎗𐎋𐎁 (rkb, “to ride, mount”), and Ge'ez ረከበ (räkäbä, “to ride; go by boat”).
The root remains productive in Modern South Arabian: compare Harsusi rēkeb (“to mount, ride”), Shehri rékəb (“to ride, mount”), and Mehri rēkēb (“to ride, mount”). Compare also Yemeni Arabic ركب (rakab, “to ride”).
The same inherited transport vocabulary underlies 𐩧𐩫𐩨𐩣 (rkbm, “rider; riding camel”), 𐩧𐩫𐩨𐩩 (rkbt, “cavalry”), 𐩣𐩧𐩫𐩨 (mrkb, “boat, ship”), and 𐩣𐩧𐩫𐩨𐩩 (mrkbt, “caravan, convoy”).

Plural pronominal-suffix-state form of 𐩧𐩫𐩨𐩣 (rkbm, “rider; riding camel”).
etymology:
A construct- and suffix-bearing form of 𐩧𐩫𐩨𐩣 (rkbm, “rider; riding camel”), itself belonging to the same Semitic √RKB riding vocabulary as the verb above.
Compare Qatabanian 𐩧𐩫𐩥𐩨 (rkwb, “horsemen; mounted troops; riders”), Akkadian rākibu (“rider; charioteer”), رَاكِب (rākib, “rider”), and رَكُوب (rakūb, “mount, riding animal”).
Modern South Arabian preserves the same semantic division between rider and mount: Harsusi rékbi (“horseman”) beside rekīb (“riding camels”), Shehri rókub (“rider”) beside ɛrkíb (“riding camel”), and Mehri rōkəb (“rider”) beside rīkēb (“riding camel”).
Ancient North Arabian provides further members of the same riding vocabulary: Safaitic 𐪇𐪋𐪈𐪉 (rkbt, “riding camel”) and Taymanitic 𐪇𐪋𐪈 (rkb, “riding camel”).

etymology:
Belongs to the Semitic root 𐩧𐩫𐩨 (rkb, “to ride”), represented across the family in words for riding, riders, mounts and vehicles. Compare Qatabanian 𐩧𐩫𐩥𐩨 (rkwb, “horsemen; mounted troops; riders”), Arabic رَاكِب (rākib, “rider; mounted person”), رَكُوب (rakūb, “mount, riding animal”), רָכַב (rakháv, “to ride”), 𐎗𐎋𐎁 (rkb, “to ride, mount”), and Akkadian rākibu (“rider; charioteer”).
The same semantic division between the rider and the ridden animal is especially well represented in Modern South Arabian: compare Harsusi rékbi (“horseman”) and rekīb (“riding camels”), Shehri rókub (“rider”) and ɛrkíb (“riding camel”), and Mehri rōkəb (“rider”) and rīkēb (“riding camel”).
Ancient North Arabian provides further parallels: Safaitic 𐪇𐪋𐪈𐪉 (rkbt, “riding camel”) and Taymanitic 𐪇𐪋𐪈 (rkb, “riding camel”).

Ancient North Arabian provides closely related riding terminology in Safaitic 𐪇𐪋𐪈𐪉 (rkbt, “riding camel”) and Taymanitic 𐪇𐪋𐪈 (rkb, “riding camel”).

glosses: To construct or establish a cistern.
etymology: A denominal verbal lexeme associated with 𐩨𐩧𐩫 (brk, “cistern, basin”).

Cognate with Qatabanian 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “to build, construct”), Minaean 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “to build, establish”), and Hadrami 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “to build, construct”).
Compare Arabic بَرَأَ (baraʔa, “to create”), بَرَى (barā, “to fashion or shape by cutting”), and Hebrew בָּרָא (bārāʾ, “to create, bring forth”). These comparisons connect the architectural vocabulary with a wider Semitic complex of making, fashioning and creation, but do not by themselves establish that all of its semantic branches have an identical history.

glosses: To build, construct, erect; to bring a structure into being.
etymology:
Cognate with Qatabanian 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “to build, construct”), Minaean 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “to build, establish”), and Hadrami 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “to build, construct”).
Compare Arabic بَرَأَ (baraʔa, “to create”), بَرَى (barā, “to fashion or shape by cutting”), and Hebrew בָּרָא (bārāʾ, “to create, bring forth”). These comparisons connect the architectural vocabulary with a wider Semitic complex of making, fashioning and creation, but do not by themselves establish that all of its semantic branches have an identical history.

glosses: To create, bring into existence, especially with a deity as subject.
etymology: A rare religious use whose relationship to the ordinary architectural verb above is disputed. Beeston regarded the divine-creation use as a borrowing, Degen and Müller compared it specifically with Hebrew בָּרָא (bārāʾ, “to create”), and Robin attributed it to Judaeo-Aramaic influence. Compare also Arabic بَرَأَ (baraʔa, “to create”).

glosses: free from responsibility, debt or liability.
etymology:
A separate legal BRʾ family concerning freedom from liability and the discharge of obligations.

Compare Arabic بَرِئَ (bariʔa, “to be free or quit of an obligation”) and بَرَّأَ (barraʔa, “to acquit, clear from liability”), as well as Yemeni Arabic barī “exempt, innocent” and baräʾ “acquit, absolve”.

glosses: To be or become free of an obligation or liability; to be discharged or cleared.

etymology:
A separate legal BRʾ family concerning freedom from liability and the discharge of obligations.
Cognate with Hadrami 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “to become free, be released”), Arabic بَرِيء (barīʔ, “free of liability, innocent”), Harsusi berīʾ (“free of debt, innocent”), Shehri bíríʾ (“free, innocent”), and Mehri bəráyʾ (“innocent, free of debt or responsibility”).

glosses: A wall or other structural work.

A feminine nominal formation of the architectural 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “to build, construct”) family.
Compare Arabic بَرَأَ (baraʔa, “to create”), بَرِيَّة (bariyya, “creation; creature”), and بَرَى (barā, “to fashion or shape by cutting”), as well as Hebrew בָּרָא (bārāʾ, “to create”).

glosses: settlement, discharge or payment of an obligation or debt.
etymology:
A nominal formation of the legal 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “to be free from liability; settle an obligation”) family.
Compare Arabic بَرَاءَة (barāʔa, “freedom from liability, acquittal, discharge”), Harsusi abrō (“to free from debt or guilt”), Jibbali bíríʾ (“to be innocent or free of obligation”), and Mehri abōri (“to free from guilt or debt”). Yemeni Arabic likewise has barāʾah ~ barāwah “freeing” and burā “clearance, receipt”.

glosses: Second-person masculine singular suffix-conjugation form of 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “to settle, discharge or pay a financial debt”).
etymology: From the legal 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “to settle, discharge or pay a financial debt”) with second-person masculine singular agreement.

etymology: Infinitive of the legal transitive 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “to settle or pay a financial debt”).

glosses: Third-person masculine dual suffix-conjugation form of 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “to build, construct”).
etymology: From 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “to build, construct”) with masculine dual agreement.

Compare Akkadian 𒂗 (bēlu, “lord, owner”), Ugaritic 𐎁𐎓𐎍 (bʿl, “lord; Baal”), Hebrew בַּעַל (baʿal, “owner, lord; Baal”), Arabic بَعْل (baʕl, “lord, husband”), Ge'ez በዓል (baʿāl, “owner, master”), Mehri mābáyl (“owned”), and Shehri báʿal (“person owning or in charge of something”).
The form is especially source-listed as part of the divine name or epithet 𐩻𐩥𐩧 𐩨𐩲𐩡𐩣 (ṯwr bʿlm, “Ṯawr Baʿlim”), whose precise interpretation is disputed.

The root is cognate with Minaean 𐩦𐩲𐩧 (s²ʿr, “to be aware”) and Arabic شَعَرَ (šaʕara, “to perceive, feel, be aware”); compare Ḥaḍramitic 𐩦𐩩𐩲𐩧 (s²tʿr, “to recognize, become aware”) and Yemeni Arabic شَعَرَ (šaʕara, “to recognize, understand, notice, perceive, feel”).

A t-derived counterpart of 𐩨𐩧𐩫 (brk, “to bless”). Robin likewise associates this Late Sabaic formation with Jewish Aramaic influence.
Compare Arabic تَبَارَكَ (tabāraka, “to be or become blessed”), Geʿez ተባረከ (tabāraka, “to receive blessing, be blessed”), Harsusi ebterōk (“to be blessed”), Shehri əbtérék (“to be blessed, happy”), and Mehri əbtərōk (“to be blessed”).

glosses: singular construct-state form of 𐩮𐩡𐩣𐩩𐩰 (ṣlmtf, “female statue; female statuette”) (shorter source-listed singular form)
singular indeterminate-state form of 𐩮𐩡𐩣𐩩𐩰 (ṣlmtf, “female statue; female statuette”)
singular determinate-state form of 𐩮𐩡𐩣𐩩𐩰 (ṣlmtf, “female statue; female statuette”)
dual indeterminate-state form of 𐩮𐩡𐩣𐩩𐩰 (ṣlmtf, “female statue; female statuette”)
plural determinate-state form of 𐩮𐩡𐩣𐩩𐩰 (ṣlmtf, “female statue; female statuette”)
A female statue, statuette, or image, especially one dedicated to a deity.
A votive female statue or cultic image in a dedication formula.
etymology:
Feminine counterpart within the 𐩮𐩡𐩣 (ṣlm) statue and image root family. Compare the masculine noun 𐩮𐩡𐩣𐩣 (ṣlmm, “male statue; male statuette”) and Qatabanian 𐩮𐩡𐩣𐩩 (ṣlmt, “female statue; statuette”).

etymology: Cognate to Ge'ez ጸሐፈ (ṣäḥäfä) Amharic ጻፈ (ṣafä), Tigrinya ጸሓፈ (ṣäḥafä). See also the Arabic ص ح ف (ṣ ḥ f).
From 𐩮𐩢𐩰 (ṣḥf, “to write”).

glosses: Discourse or progress particle marking continuation from a preceding clause, phrase, or situation; often left untranslated in English.
then, so, therefore; marking the main clause or result after a preceding condition, subordinate clause, or narrative setup.
now, as for, so then; introducing a new main statement, especially after 𐩠𐩱 (hʾ).
In legal or prescriptive contexts, marking consequence, alternative, or what follows if the preceding clause applies.
etymology: Compare فَـ (fa-, “and then, so, therefore”). Sabaweb describes the Amiritic use of 𐩰 (f-) as equivalent to Arabic فَـ (fa-), but the ordinary Sabaean function is broader and often more discourse-like than a simple conjunction.

glosses: singular construct-state form of 𐩰𐩧𐩪𐩣 (frs¹m, “horse; horseman”)
singular form of 𐩰𐩧𐩪𐩣 (frs¹m, “horse; horseman”) in the pronominal-suffix state
etymology:
A state form of 𐩰𐩧𐩪𐩣 (frs¹m, “horse; horseman”).
The underlying lexeme is cognate with Arabic فَرَس (faras, “horse, mare”) and Ge'ez ፈረስ (färäs, “horse”). Compare Ḥaḍramitic 𐩱𐩰𐩧𐩪 (ʾfrs¹, “cavalry”) and Yemeni Arabic فَرَس (faras, “mare”).

glosses: A representation of a horse, especially a horse statuette or other votive image.
A horseman, mounted rider or member of a cavalry force, especially in the plural.
etymology:
Belongs to a widespread Semitic equestrian word-family. Cognate with Arabic فَرَس (faras, “horse, mare”) and Ge'ez ፈረስ (färäs, “horse”). Compare Ḥaḍramitic 𐩱𐩰𐩧𐩪 (ʾfrs¹, “cavalry”), Safaitic frs “horse; horseman”, and Yemeni Arabic فَرَس (faras, “mare”).
The human sense belongs to the same equestrian family; compare فَارِس (fāris, “horseman, rider”) and Yemeni Arabic فَارِس (fāris, “rider”). Mehri fərháyn and Ḥarsusi ferhīn, both “mare; horse”, provide further Modern South Arabian parallels, though with a different final radical.
The Sabaean plural stem 𐩱𐩰𐩧𐩪 (ʾfrs¹) closely resembles Arabic أَفْرَاس (ʔafrās, “horses”), the broken plural of فَرَس (faras).

glosses: singular determinate-state form of 𐩰𐩧𐩪𐩣 (frs¹m, “horse; horseman”)
etymology:
From 𐩰𐩧𐩪𐩣 (frs¹m, “horse; horseman”) with the Sabaean determinate-state ending -n.
The lexical base is cognate with Arabic فَرَس (faras, “horse, mare”) and Ge'ez ፈረስ (färäs, “horse”); compare Ḥaḍramitic 𐩱𐩰𐩧𐩪 (ʾfrs¹, “cavalry”) and Yemeni Arabic فَرَس (faras, “mare”).

glosses: people; persons belonging to a place, group, household, or community.
clan; family group; lineage or descent group.
community; corporate group; body of people acting together.
religious or cultic community; community attached to a deity or sanctuary.
tribal group; section of a tribe; inhabitants or members of a named group.
etymology:
From Proto-Semitic *ʔahl- (“tent; household”). The Sabaean sense developed in the social direction “household, people belonging together” > “people, clan, community”. Compare Arabic أَهْل (ʔahl, “family, people, inhabitants”), Hebrew אֹהֶל (ʾōhel, “tent”), and Aramaic אהלא (ʾahlā, “tent”).

glosses: prohibitive or negative particle before a verbal form; do not, let not, may not.
negative particle in penitential, legal, and declarative clauses.
not; no, especially in paired or contrastive expressions.
etymology: From an inherited Semitic negative particle. Compare Hebrew אַל (ʾal, “do not”), Jewish Aramaic אַל (ʾal, “not; do not”), and Arabic لَا (lā, “not”) in the broader Semitic negative-particle system.

glosses: plural relative pronoun; those who; those which.
etymology: Probably a plural form of the relative pronoun 𐩹 (ḏ-, “who; which; of”), following Prioletta’s interpretation cited by Sabaweb. Older interpretations treated the construction as “whether ... or”, “either ... or”, or similar, but the local penitential context supports a relative reading.

glosses: Source-listed singular form of 𐩱𐩡𐩣 (ʾlm, “god; deity”), especially in construct and pronominal-suffix contexts.
god, deity; especially as the possessed or construct form of a deity term.
etymology: From 𐩱𐩡𐩣 (ʾlm, “god; deity”), as a shorter source-listed nominal form. Ultimately from Proto-Semitic *ʾil- (“god, deity”).
From Proto-Semitic *ʔil-.

glosses: patron deity of a person, family, city, tribe, or group.
God; the God, especially in the determinate form 𐩱𐩡𐩬 (ʾln).
etymology:
From Proto-Semitic *ʔil- (“god, deity”). Compare Akkadian 𒀭 (ilum, “god”), Ugaritic 𐎛𐎍 (ʾil, “god”), Hebrew אֵל (ʾēl, “god”), Arabic إِلٰه (ʔilāh, “god, deity”), and Aramaic אֱלָהָא (ʾĕlāhā, “God, deity”). Also compare Qatabanian 𐩱𐩡 (ʾl, “god, deity”) and Minaic 𐩱𐩡 (ʾl, “god, deity”).

glosses: ritual banquet; feast, especially a cultic meal or banquet.
etymology:
Uncertain. Sabaweb treats this as a separate root 𐩱𐩡𐩣 (ʾlm) connected with ritual banqueting. It has been compared with banquet and feast vocabulary such as Arabic وَلِيمَة (walīma, “feast, banquet”), Arabic أَوْلَمَ (ʔawlama, “to give a banquet”), Hassaniya Arabic awōləm (“to prepare, especially food”), and Harsusi awlōm (“to prepare a meal”), but the exact historical relationship is not secure.

glosses: Almaqah, especially as invoked with cultic or local epithets.
A cultic epithet of 𐩱𐩡𐩣𐩤𐩠 (ʾlmqh, “ʾAlmaqah”), associated with 𐩮𐩧𐩥𐩢 (Ṣrwḥ, “Ṣirwāḥ”).
etymology: From 𐩱𐩡𐩣𐩤𐩠 (ʾlmqh, “ʾAlmaqah”) + 𐩨𐩲𐩡 (bʿl, “lord, master”) + the plural construct 𐩱𐩥𐩲𐩡 (ʾwʿl, “ibexes”) + 𐩮𐩧𐩥𐩢 (Ṣrwḥ, “Ṣirwāḥ”). Literally “ʾAlmaqah, Lord of the Ibexes of Ṣirwāḥ”.

glosses: one’s goddesses; female deities of a person, family, tribe, or group.
female divine powers; goddesses as a divine group, especially in invocations and protective formulae.
etymology:
From Proto-Semitic *ʔil- (“god, deity”), with feminine 𐩩 (-t). Compare Akkadian 𒀭 (iltu, “goddess”), Ugaritic 𐎛𐎍𐎚 (ʾilt, “goddess”), Arabic إِلٰهَة (ʔilāha, “goddess”), and Safaitic ʾlt “goddess”. Also compare Qatabanian 𐩱𐩡𐩩 (ʾlt, “goddess”) and Minaic 𐩱𐩡𐩩 (ʾlt, “goddess”).

glosses: Indeterminate plural form of 𐩱𐩡𐩩 (ʾlt, “goddess, female deity”); goddesses, female deities.

Masculine plural near-deictic demonstrative pronoun: these, these ones, the following.
etymology: From the Sabaean near-demonstrative series built on 𐩹 (ḏ-). Sabaweb lists ʾln under the masculine demonstrative lemma ḏnm, specifically as a masculine plural form.

glosses: singular determinate-state form of 𐩱𐩡𐩣 (ʾlm, “god; male deity”).
etymology: Determinate singular form of 𐩱𐩡𐩣 (ʾlm, “god; male deity”).
See Arabic الْحَبَشَة (al-ḥabaša)

glosses: mother of a deity; divine mother, especially in theonymic or cultic epithets.
used in divine names and epithets such as 𐩱𐩣𐩲𐩻𐩩𐩧 (ʾmʿṯtr, “Mother of ʿṯtr”).
etymology:
From Proto-Semitic *ʔimm- (“mother”). Compare Arabic أُمّ (ʔumm, “mother”), Hebrew אֵם (ʾem, “mother”), Ge'ez እም (ʾəmm, “mother”), and Akkadian 𒌝𒈪 (ummu, “mother”).

glosses: or; whether; disjunctive particle, especially before the second member of an alternative or double question.
etymology: Compare Arabic أَم (ʔam, “or”), Hebrew אִם (ʾim, “if; whether”), and Jewish Aramaic אִם (ʾim, “if; whether”).

glosses: relatives, close associates, people standing in a close relationship; perhaps allies.
etymology:
A social plural formation of the QRB vocabulary of nearness and close relationship.
Compare Akkadian qerbu (“close person, relative”), Arabic أَقْرَبُون (ʔaqrabūn, “relatives, near ones”), Geʿez qərubāwi (“one who is close”), Harsusi ḳeréb (“near”), Shehri ḳéríb (“near; relation”), and Mehri ḳəráyb (“near, nearly”).

A separate nominal formation associated with the QRB lexical family. Its precise derivation and documentary function are uncertain.
Compare Akkadian 𒆪𒉡 (qerēbu, “to approach; in the D-stem, to bring near”), Arabic قَرِبَ (qariba, “to be near, approach”), Geʿez ቀረበ (ḳäräbä, “to be near, approach”), and the corresponding causative vocabulary of bringing or presenting.

glosses: plural construct-state form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩣 (qnym, “possession, property”)
plural form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩣 (qnym, “possession, property”) in the pronominal-suffix state
etymology: Plural stem of 𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩣 (qnym, “possession, property”), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”).

glosses: plural indeterminate-state form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “small livestock, sheep”)
etymology: An indeterminate plural form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺 (qny, “small livestock, sheep”).

glosses: plural indeterminate-state form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩣 (qnym, “possession, property”)
etymology: From the plural stem 𐩱𐩤𐩬𐩺 (ʾqny) of 𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩣 (qnym, “possession, property”), with the indeterminate-state ending -m. Ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”).

glosses: singular construct-state form of 𐩱𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩩𐩣 (ʾqnytm, “dedication, votive offering”)
singular form of 𐩱𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩩𐩣 (ʾqnytm, “dedication, votive offering”) in the pronominal-suffix state
plural construct-state form of 𐩱𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩩𐩣 (ʾqnytm, “dedication, votive offering”)
etymology: A state form of 𐩱𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩩𐩣 (ʾqnytm, “dedication, votive offering”), a variant member of the QNY dedicatory family, ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”).

A separate, poorly attested noun related to the QNY possession vocabulary, ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”). A semantic development through persons treated as property has been proposed, but the sole surviving attestation is uncertain.

glosses: dedication, votive offering; something formally dedicated or consecrated.
etymology:
A variant dedicatory noun beside 𐩠𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩩 (hqnyt, “dedication, votive offering”), belonging to the QNY dedicatory family and ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”).
Sabaweb explicitly describes the formation as a genuine variant of 𐩠𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩩 (hqnyt) meaning simply “dedication”.

glosses: singular determinate-state form of 𐩱𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩩𐩣 (ʾqnytm, “dedication, votive offering”)
etymology: From 𐩱𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩩𐩣 (ʾqnytm, “dedication, votive offering”) with the determinate-state ending -n. The parent noun belongs to the QNY dedicatory family, ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”).

glosses: plural determinate-state form of 𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩣 (qnym, “possession, property”)
etymology: From the plural stem 𐩱𐩤𐩬𐩺 (ʾqny) of 𐩤𐩬𐩺𐩣 (qnym, “possession, property”), with the determinate-state ending -n. Ultimately from Proto-Semitic *q-n-y (“to acquire, possess”).

glosses: or; marking an alternative between words, phrases, or clauses.
or; especially in ritual, legal, or prescriptive alternatives.
or else, otherwise; especially after 𐩰 (f-) in legal or consequential clauses.
In paired constructions, marking alternatives: either ... or, whether ... or, be it ... or.
etymology: Cognate with Arabic أَوْ (ʔaw, “or”), Hebrew אוֹ (ʾō, “or”), Ge'ez አው (ʾaw, “or”), Mehri ʾaw (“or”), and Harsusi ʾaw (“or”). Compare also Akkadian ū (“or”).

plural indeterminate-state form of 𐩥𐩲𐩡𐩣 (wʿlm, “ibex; ibex statuette”)
plural determinate-state form of 𐩥𐩲𐩡𐩣 (wʿlm, “ibex; ibex statuette”)
ancestral group; lineage; family or clan group, especially in forms such as 𐩱𐩨𐩥𐩩 (ʾbwt).

glosses: plural construct-state form of 𐩨𐩧𐩥𐩣 (brwm, “son, child”)
etymology:
The plural construct of 𐩨𐩧𐩥𐩣 (brwm, “son, child”), with the plural stem in ʾbrw-. Minaean has a closely corresponding plural ʾbrw- “sons, children”.
The underlying kinship lexeme belongs with Aramaic בר (bar, “son”), Classical Syriac ܒܪܐ (brā, “son”), Mehri bər (“son”), and Harsusi ber (“son”).

glosses: plural construct-state form of 𐩨𐩧𐩫 (brk, “cistern, basin”)
plural form of 𐩨𐩧𐩫 (brk, “cistern, basin”) in the pronominal-suffix state
etymology: Plural formation of 𐩨𐩧𐩫 (brk, “cistern, basin”).

glosses: plural construct-state form of 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “construction work”)
etymology: Plural formation of 𐩨𐩧𐩱 (brʾ, “construction work”).
From Proto-Semitic *ʔabn-.

glosses: plural form of 𐩨𐩲𐩡 (bʿl, “lord; owner”); lords; owners.
inhabitants; citizens; members of a town, house, lineage, or corporate group.
owners or members of; those belonging to a named house, town, estate, or group.
one’s household members, dependants, or members of one’s house.
parties, holders, or persons with standing in a property, town, or communal matter.
etymology:
Plural of 𐩨𐩲𐩡 (bʿl, “lord; owner; inhabitant”), from the root 𐩨𐩲𐩡 (bʿl, “to own; possess; be lord of”), ultimately from Proto-Semitic *baʿl- (“owner; lord; master”).
Compare Akkadian 𒂗 (bēlu, “lord, owner”), Ugaritic 𐎁𐎓𐎍 (bʿl, “lord; Baal”), Hebrew בַּעַל (baʿal, “owner, lord”), Arabic بَعْل (baʕl, “lord, husband”), Ge'ez በዓል (baʿāl, “owner, master”), Mehri mābáyl (“owned”), and Shehri báʿal (“person owning or in charge of something”).

glosses: plural construct-state form of 𐩨𐩺𐩩 (byt, “house; household; palace; temple”)
plural form of 𐩨𐩺𐩩 (byt, “house; household; palace; temple”) in the pronominal-suffix state
houses; households; family houses; corporate house-groups.
etymology:
From 𐩨𐩺𐩩 (byt, “house; household; palace; temple”), from Proto-Semitic *bayt- (“house”).
Although Sabaweb uses bytm as the lemma label for the noun family, the Wiktionary lemma is the base form 𐩨𐩺𐩩 (byt). The plural series includes 𐩱𐩨𐩺𐩩 (ʾbyt), 𐩱𐩨𐩺𐩩𐩣 (ʾbytm), and 𐩱𐩨𐩺𐩩𐩬 (ʾbytn).

glosses: plural indeterminate-state form of 𐩨𐩺𐩩 (byt, “house; household; palace; temple”)
houses; house-buildings; palace-buildings; estates, according to context.
etymology:
From 𐩨𐩺𐩩 (byt, “house; household; palace; temple”), from Proto-Semitic *bayt- (“house”).
Although Sabaweb uses bytm as the lemma label for the wider noun family, the Wiktionary lemma is 𐩨𐩺𐩩 (byt). The form 𐩱𐩨𐩺𐩩𐩣 (ʾbytm) is the plural indeterminate form.

glosses: plural determinate-state form of 𐩨𐩺𐩩 (byt, “house; household; palace; temple”)
the houses; the households; the corporate houses or house-groups in question.
etymology: From 𐩨𐩺𐩩 (byt, “house; household; palace; temple”), from Proto-Semitic *bayt- (“house”).
From Proto-Semitic *ʔakal- (“food”).

glosses: female; female person or animal, especially as opposed to male.
women; wives; female members of a household, family, clan, or community.

glosses: kinsman; male relative; clan-fellow or member of the same lineage or social group.
brothers; kinsmen; fellow members of a family, clan, or group.
ally; sworn brother; confederate; partner in a pact or alliance.

glosses: plural construct-state form of 𐩮𐩡𐩣𐩣 (ṣlmm, “male statue; male statuette”)

etymology:
The unmarked plural stem of 𐩰𐩧𐩪𐩣 (frs¹m, “horse; horseman”).
It has a close morphological and lexical parallel in Arabic أَفْرَاس (ʔafrās, “horses”), plural of فَرَس (faras, “horse, mare”). Ḥaḍramitic has the same consonantal plural 𐩱𐩰𐩧𐩪 (ʾfrs¹, “cavalry”).

glosses: plural indeterminate-state form of 𐩰𐩧𐩪𐩣 (frs¹m, “horse; horseman”)
etymology:
From the plural stem 𐩱𐩰𐩧𐩪 (ʾfrs¹) of 𐩰𐩧𐩪𐩣 (frs¹m, “horse; horseman”), with the indeterminate-state ending -m.
The plural stem has a particularly close parallel in Arabic أَفْرَاس (ʔafrās, “horses”), plural of فَرَس (faras, “horse, mare”). Compare also Ḥaḍramitic 𐩱𐩰𐩧𐩪 (ʾfrs¹, “cavalry”).

glosses: plural determinate-state form of 𐩰𐩧𐩪𐩣 (frs¹m, “horse; horseman”)
etymology:
From the plural stem 𐩱𐩰𐩧𐩪 (ʾfrs¹) of 𐩰𐩧𐩪𐩣 (frs¹m, “horse; horseman”) with the determinate-state ending -n.
Compare Arabic أَفْرَاس (ʔafrās, “horses”) and the closely corresponding Ḥaḍramitic 𐩱𐩰𐩧𐩪 (ʾfrs¹, “cavalry”).

plural indeterminate-state form of 𐩹𐩠𐩨 (ḏhb, “flood-water; irrigation flow”)

singular form of 𐩱𐩬𐩻𐩩 (ʾnṯt, “woman; wife”) in the pronominal-suffix state
wife, especially in expressions with pronominal suffixes.
etymology: Shorter form of 𐩱𐩬𐩻𐩩 (ʾnṯt, “woman; wife”), from Proto-Semitic *ʔanṯ-at- (“woman; wife”). Compare Arabic أُنْثَى (ʔunṯā, “female”), Akkadian 𒊩 (aššatu, “wife”), and Ge'ez አንስት (ʾanəst, “woman”). The shortened Sabaean spelling ʾṯt is especially useful to record because it appears in personal, familial, and pronominal-suffix contexts.

glosses: elder male relative; paternal or ancestral male relation.
etymology:
From Proto-Semitic *ʕamm- (“paternal uncle; male kinsman”). Compare Arabic عَمّ (ʕamm, “paternal uncle”), Hebrew עַם (ʿam, “kinsman; people”), Safaitic 𐪒𐪑 (ʿm, “paternal grandfather”), and Modern South Arabian forms such as Mehri ʾōm “ancestor, grandfather”.

glosses: with; together with; in company with.
in the presence of; before; at the side of.
from; from the side of; on the authority of, especially in transactions or formulaic legal contexts.
against, especially in military or adversative contexts.
etymology: From an inherited Semitic prepositional base; compare Hebrew עִם (ʿim, “with”), Aramaic עִם (ʿim, “with”), and related Semitic forms meaning “with” or “together with”.
From Proto-Semitic *ʕiṣ́-.

glosses: relative; kinsman; person belonging to or attached to a family, household, or clan.
affinal relative; in-law; relative by marriage or social attachment.
dependant; client; protected or affiliated person attached to a household, clan, or corporate group.
relatives; affiliates; dependants; protected persons; persons attached to a family, clan, or legal group.
etymology:
Uncertain. Probably connected with a Semitic root *ʕḏr- (“to help, protect, excuse, hold back”) or a related social-legal base denoting protection, affiliation, or dependence, but the exact inherited form is not secure.
Compare Qatabanian ʿḏr, especially in expressions with ḏ-, “dependent, protected person, affiliated person”, and Epigraphic Ethiopic ʿḏr, “dependants, clients”. Further compare Arabic عُذْر (ʕuḏr, “excuse, plea”), Arabic اِعْتَذَرَ (iʕtaḏara, “to excuse oneself”), Ḥarsusi šāḏōr “to excuse oneself”, Jibbali saʿḏér “to excuse oneself; refuse; refrain”, and Mehri hāḏōr / šāḏōr “to excuse oneself; refrain; refuse”. Older comparisons with Hebrew עֵזֶר (ʿēzer, “help, aid”) are semantically suggestive but should be treated as comparison, not proof.

glosses: to pursue; to go after; to follow up a matter.
to seek redress; to bring to account; to exact reprisals.
etymology:
Uncertain. Probably connected with a Semitic root *ʕḏr- (“to help, protect, excuse, hold back”) or a related social-legal base denoting protection, affiliation, or dependence, but the exact inherited form is not secure.
Compare Qatabanian ʿḏr, especially in expressions with ḏ-, “dependent, protected person, affiliated person”, and Epigraphic Ethiopic ʿḏr, “dependants, clients”. Further compare Arabic عُذْر (ʕuḏr, “excuse, plea”), Arabic اِعْتَذَرَ (iʕtaḏara, “to excuse oneself”), Ḥarsusi šāḏōr “to excuse oneself”, Jibbali saʿḏér “to excuse oneself; refuse; refrain”, and Mehri hāḏōr / šāḏōr “to excuse oneself; refrain; refuse”. Older comparisons with Hebrew עֵזֶר (ʿēzer, “help, aid”) are semantically suggestive but should be treated as comparison, not proof.

glosses: ʿAthtar; a major South Arabian deity.
a named manifestation or local form of ʿAthtar, especially with divine epithets such as 𐩹𐩨𐩬 (Ḏbn), 𐩦𐩧𐩤𐩬 (S²rqn), 𐩴𐩧𐩨 (Grb), and 𐩧𐩮𐩰 (Rṣf).
a deity invoked in protection, curse, oath, dedication, and thanksgiving formulae.
divine-name element in personal names, titles, epithets, and sanctuary names.
etymology:
From the wider Semitic divine-name complex *ʿṯtr / *ʿštr. Compare Akkadian 𒀭𒈹 (Ištar, “Ishtar”), Ugaritic 𐎓𐎘𐎚𐎗 (ʿṯtr, “ʿAthtar”), Hebrew עַשְׁתֹּרֶת (ʿaštōreṯ, “Astarte”), and Arabic عَثْتَر (ʕaṯtar, “ʿAthtar”). Also compare Minaic 𐩲𐩻𐩩𐩧 (ʿṯtr, “ʿAthtar”), Qatabanian 𐩲𐩻𐩩𐩧 (ʿṯtr, “ʿAthtar”), and Ḥaḍramitic 𐩲𐩻𐩩𐩧 (ʿṯtr, “ʿAthtar”).

From Proto-Semitic *dam-.
Cognate to Arabic غُنْم (ḡunm).
Cognate with Arabic طِيب (ṭīb, “perfume”).

glosses: determinative or genitive-linking clitic; of, belonging to, associated with.
marker of clan, lineage, house, or group affiliation; of, from, belonging to.
element introducing or forming names of deities, places, lineages, tribes, and corporate groups.
etymology: From a Semitic deictic and relative base. Compare Ge'ez ዘ (za, “of; which; who”), Arabic ذُو (ḏū, “possessor of; one of”), and Hebrew Hebrew זֶה (ze, “this”). Also compare Qatabanian 𐩹 (ḏ-, “of; who; which”), Minaic 𐩹 (ḏ-, “of; who; which”), and Ḥaḍramitic 𐩹 (ḏ-, “of; who; which”).

glosses: bronze, especially as the material of a votive offering, statue, plaque, or cultic object.
A bronze object, bronze fitting, or bronze element in a dedication or object list.
etymology:
From a Semitic precious-metal word. Compare Arabic ذَهَب (ḏahab, “gold”), Hebrew זָהָב (zāhāḇ, “gold”), Jewish Aramaic דַּהֲבָא (dahăḇā, “gold”), and Mehri ḏəhēb (“bronze”). In Sabaean dedicatory inscriptions, the usual object-material meaning is “bronze”, not ordinary “gold”.
Sabaean root family 𐩹𐩠𐩨 (ḏhb) — bronze; bronze ornamentation; flood-water; oasis; grain measure

 𐩹𐩠𐩨 (ḏhb) — bronze; bronze ornamentation; flood-water; oasis; grain measure
 Type homographic triradical root family
 Radicals 𐩹 (ḏ) · 𐩠 (h) · 𐩨 (b)
 Semantic field bronze; votive objects; metalwork; irrigation; oases; grain measures
 Sabaean terms and comparisons
 Core terms 𐩹𐩠𐩨 (ḏhb, “bronze; capacity measure”), 𐩹𐩠𐩨𐩣 (ḏhbm, “bronze; oasis; flood; measure”), 𐩹𐩠𐩨𐩬 (ḏhbn, “the bronze; the ḏhb-measure”)
 Nominal derivatives 𐩩𐩹𐩠𐩨 (tḏhb, “bronze ornamentation”), 𐩣𐩹𐩠𐩨𐩩 (mḏhbt, “irrigation structure”), 𐩱𐩹𐩠𐩨 (ʾḏhb), 𐩱𐩹𐩠𐩨𐩣 (ʾḏhbm), 𐩱𐩹𐩠𐩨𐩬 (ʾḏhbn)
 Forms and variants 𐩹𐩠𐩨𐩬 (ḏhbn) is especially common as a determinate/material form. 𐩹𐩠𐩨𐩣 (ḏhbm) is shared by the bronze, flood, oasis, and measure entries. 𐩱𐩹𐩠𐩨 (ʾḏhb) is used in plural, construct, and suffixal contexts.
 Related terms 𐩮𐩡𐩣𐩣 (ṣlmm, “statue”), 𐩻𐩥𐩧𐩣 (ṯwrm, “bull; bull statuette”), 𐩥𐩲𐩡𐩣 (wʿlm, “ibex; ibex statuette”), 𐩠𐩤𐩬𐩺 (hqny, “to dedicate”)
 Compare Arabic ذَهَب (ḏahab, “gold”), Hebrew זָהָב (zāhāḇ, “gold”), Mehri ḏəhēb (“bronze; flood-water”)
Note: This root is strongly homographic. The bronze noun dominates dedicatory object texts, while separate source entries cover an aromatic substance, a bronze-decoration verb, flood-water, oasis or irrigated land, a grain measure, bronze ornamentation, and an irrigation structure.

glosses: A rare, not precisely identifiable aromatic substance; ḏahab-aroma.
etymology: A rare source-separated aromatic use. It may be connected with the colour or precious-material word in Etymology 1, but the inscriptional meaning is treated separately.

glosses: To furnish with bronze elements; to decorate or ornament with bronze.
etymology: Denominative from the bronze/material noun in Etymology 1.

glosses: A flood, flood-water, rain-stream, or irrigation flow.
Irrigation water used in agricultural land.
etymology: From a water and flooding semantic field. Compare Arabic ḏihba “rain shower”, Ḥarsusi ḏehīb “flood-water, stream”, Jibbali ḏhéb “flood torrent”, and Mehri ḏəhīb “flood-water, torrent”.

glosses: singular construct-state form of 𐩹𐩠𐩨𐩣 (ḏhbm, “oasis; river valley; irrigation area”)
singular form of 𐩹𐩠𐩨𐩣 (ḏhbm, “oasis; river valley; irrigation area”) in the pronominal-suffix state
etymology: A form belonging to the oasis and irrigated-land noun 𐩹𐩠𐩨𐩣 (ḏhbm). The semantic field overlaps with Etymology 4 but Sabaweb treats the oasis/irrigated-area noun separately.

glosses: A dry capacity measure, especially for grain.
etymology: A source-separated measure noun, probably connected with the Yemeni Arabic measure word rather than with the bronze noun. Sabaweb compares Arabic ḏahab “a certain measure of capacity for corn, used in Yemen”, Yemeni Arabic ḏahb “a dry measure”, and Yemeni Arabic ḏahb “a dry measure of about 24 litres, though not constant everywhere”.

glosses: singular indeterminate-state form of 𐩹𐩠𐩨 (ḏhb, “flood-water; irrigation flow”)
singular indeterminate-state form of 𐩹𐩠𐩨 (ḏhb, “capacity measure for grain”)
etymology: Form of 𐩹𐩠𐩨 (ḏhb) in several homographic entries.

glosses: An oasis, river valley, alluvial valley, or irrigated agricultural area.
A cultivated or irrigated zone, especially in a desert or wadi environment.
etymology: From the water and irrigation semantic field of 𐩹𐩠𐩨 (ḏhb), but source-listed as a separate noun meaning “oasis, river valley, irrigation area”.

glosses: Used in material phrases meaning “of bronze”.
singular determinate-state form of 𐩹𐩠𐩨 (ḏhb, “flood-water; irrigation flow”)
singular determinate-state form of 𐩹𐩠𐩨𐩣 (ḏhbm, “oasis; river valley; irrigation area”)
singular determinate-state form of 𐩹𐩠𐩨 (ḏhb, “capacity measure for grain”)
dual indeterminate-state form of 𐩹𐩠𐩨 (ḏhb, “capacity measure for grain”)
dual construct-state form of 𐩹𐩠𐩨𐩣 (ḏhbm, “oasis; river valley; irrigation area”)
clause-introducing particle; that, especially introducing a subordinate clause.
in the construction 𐩫𐩹𐩣 (k-ḏ-m), introducing the content of an oath, declaration, report, or legal undertaking.
determinative or relative clause marker, overlapping in function with 𐩹 (ḏ-) and 𐩹𐩩 (ḏt).
etymology: From the same deictic and relative base as 𐩹 (ḏ-, “who; which; of”) and 𐩹𐩩 (ḏt, “that; this”), with enclitic 𐩣 (-m). Compare Ge'ez ዘ (za, “of; which; who”) and Arabic ذَا (ḏā, “this”).

glosses: some of; certain among; a number from a larger group.
part of; a portion of, especially of land, territory, buildings, groups, or property.
one or more persons, places, or things from a named group.
etymology: From 𐩹 (ḏ-, “who; which; of”) + 𐩨𐩬 (bn, “from; out of”). The construction is partitive: “one/some of”, “part of”, or “certain among”.

glosses: purpose-introducing particle; so that, in order that.
formulaic particle in dedicatory thanksgiving and request clauses, especially after 𐩨 (b-, “by; because of”) and 𐩡 (l-, “for; so that”).
etymology: From the same Semitic deictic and relative base as 𐩹 (ḏ-, “who; which; of”), with feminine 𐩩 (-t). Compare Ge'ez ዘ (za, “of; which; who”), Arabic ذَات (ḏāt, “possessor of; ذات”), and Yemeni Arabic ذِي (ḏī, “this, feminine”). Also compare Qatabanian 𐩹𐩩 (ḏt, “that; this; which”), Minaic 𐩹𐩩 (ḏt, “that; this; which”), and Ḥaḍramitic 𐩹𐩩 (ḏt, “that; this; which”).

glosses: feminine demonstrative pronoun; this, this one.
feminine relative or determinative pronoun; which, that, of.
marker of feminine affiliation; she of, woman of, belonging to a family, clan, or house.
this; the present, especially in references to a dedication, inscription, object, or legal act.
etymology: From the same Semitic deictic and relative base as 𐩹 (ḏ-, “who; which; of”), with feminine 𐩩 (-t). Compare Ge'ez ዘ (za, “of; which; who”), Arabic ذَات (ḏāt, “possessor of; ذات”), and Yemeni Arabic ذِي (ḏī, “this, feminine”). Also compare Qatabanian 𐩹𐩩 (ḏt, “that; this; which”), Minaic 𐩹𐩩 (ḏt, “that; this; which”), and Ḥaḍramitic 𐩹𐩩 (ḏt, “that; this; which”).

glosses: feminine demonstrative form; this, this one.
these, especially in southern or dialectal contexts.
etymology: Variant or extended demonstrative form related to 𐩹𐩩 (ḏt, “this; feminine demonstrative”) and 𐩹𐩬 (ḏn, “this; masculine demonstrative”). Sabaweb notes that the distribution may reflect a regional or dialectal feature, especially in southern material, and compares Qatabanian 𐩹𐩩𐩬 (ḏtn, “this; these”).

glosses: record, mention, the mental state or act of recollecting
a record or mention that has been issued, declaration, notification, report; rumour
etymology: From Proto-Semitic *ḏikar-.

glosses: to mention, to record, to register
etymology: From Proto-Semitic *ḏikar-.

glosses: masculine demonstrative pronoun; this, this one.
demonstrative determiner with masculine nouns; this.
demonstrative reference to an inscription, object, act, dedication, building, or legal matter just mentioned.
etymology:
From the Semitic deictic base also seen in 𐩹 (ḏ-, “who; which; of”) and 𐩹𐩩 (ḏt, “this; that; because”). Compare Arabic ذَا (ḏā, “this”), Yemeni Arabic ذَا (ḏā, “this”), and Ge'ez ዝ (zə, “this”).
Sabaweb uses the lemma label ḏnm, but the source-listed Sabaean form is normally ḏn.

glosses: Masculine dual oblique form of the near demonstrative: these two, this pair.
etymology: Belongs to the Sabaean near-demonstrative series built on 𐩹 (ḏ-). Sabaweb lists the form under the masculine demonstrative lemma ḏnm, with ḏyn specifically labelled as a masculine dual oblique form in Fa 71/3.

glosses: A bull-associated divine name or divine epithet, especially in the cultic expression 𐩻𐩥𐩧 𐩨𐩲𐩡𐩣 (ṯwr bʿlm).
etymology:
From Proto-Semitic *ṯawr- (“bull, ox”). Compare Arabic ثَوْر (ṯawr, “bull, ox”), Hebrew שׁוֹר (šōr, “ox, bull”), and Classical Syriac ܬܘܪܐ (tawrā, “ox, bull”).
The same word also appears in cultic and theonymic use, especially in the divine title or name 𐩻𐩥𐩧 𐩨𐩲𐩡𐩣 (ṯwr bʿlm).

glosses: A Sabaean divine title or divine name, invoked with other deities in cultic formulae.
etymology: From 𐩻𐩥𐩧 (ṯwr, “bull; divine epithet”) + 𐩨𐩲𐩡𐩣 (bʿlm). Literally “Bull of Bʿlm/Baʿlum”, but used as a fixed cultic title or divine name.

glosses: A bull statuette or bull-shaped votive offering, especially one dedicated to a deity.
etymology:
From Proto-Semitic *ṯawr- (“bull, ox”). Compare Arabic ثَوْر (ṯawr, “bull, ox”), Hebrew שׁוֹר (šōr, “ox, bull”), and Classical Syriac ܬܘܪܐ (tawrā, “ox, bull”).
Sabaean root family 𐩻𐩥𐩧 (ṯwr) — bull; bull statuette
 Root profile
 Root
 𐩻𐩥𐩧 (ṯwr) — bull; bull statuette
 Type triradical animal and votive-object noun
 Radicals 𐩻 (ṯ) · 𐩥 (w) · 𐩧 (r)
 Proto-Semitic comparison *ṯawr- (“bull, ox”)
 Semantic field bulls; bovines; animal offerings; votive objects; cultic dedications
 Sabaean terms and comparisons
 Core terms 𐩻𐩥𐩧𐩣 (ṯwrm, “bull; bull statuette”)
 Nominal derivatives 𐩻𐩥𐩧 (ṯwr, “bull”), 𐩻𐩧 (ṯr, “bull”), 𐩻𐩥𐩧𐩬 (ṯwrn, “the bull; two bulls”), 𐩱𐩻𐩥𐩧𐩣 (ʾṯwrm, “bulls”), 𐩱𐩻𐩥𐩧𐩬 (ʾṯwrn, “the bulls”)
 Forms and variants 𐩻𐩥𐩧𐩣 (ṯwrm) is the common indeterminate singular form. 𐩻𐩥𐩧𐩬 (ṯwrn) is used both for the determinate singular and the indeterminate dual. Shorter construct and pronominal forms include 𐩻𐩥𐩧 (ṯwr) and 𐩻𐩧 (ṯr). Plural forms include 𐩱𐩻𐩥𐩧𐩣 (ʾṯwrm) and 𐩱𐩻𐩥𐩧𐩬 (ʾṯwrn).
 Related terms 𐩮𐩡𐩣𐩣 (ṣlmm, “male statue; male statuette”), 𐩮𐩡𐩣𐩩𐩰 (ṣlmtf, “female statue; female statuette”), 𐩥𐩲𐩡𐩣 (wʿlm, “ibex”), 𐩠𐩤𐩬𐩺 (hqny, “to dedicate, consecrate”), 𐩹𐩠𐩨𐩣 (ḏhbm, “bronze”)
 Compare Arabic ثَوْر (ṯawr, “bull, ox”), Hebrew שׁוֹר (šōr, “ox, bull”), Classical Syriac ܬܘܪܐ (tawrā, “ox, bull”)
Note: The noun denotes a real bull or a bull-shaped votive object. In dedicatory texts it often appears beside statues and other offerings; in military or property contexts it may refer to cattle or bovines more generally.
